summary: Summarizes issues around the routing and addressing scaling problems in the IP architecture and gives background on the ROAD group and related activities in the IETF. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1380 describes how Internet growth was stressing address allocation and routing in 1992. The Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) records immediate steps and further study of ways to provide more addresses.

subtitle: An IESG report on Internet routing growth, address limits and a phased response.

tldr.problem: Internet growth was straining the supply of Class B network numbers and the ability of routers and operators to manage routing information. The RFC also treats exhaustion of the IP address space as a longer-term concern.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG summarizes ROAD group work and recommends immediate operational measures, short-term routing improvements including CIDR, and parallel evaluation of larger address proposals.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational report of the IESG's deliberations and proposed work, not a protocol specification. The RFC supports CIDR work while calling for further evaluation of larger addresses.

facts.label: Class B allocation estimate
facts.value: Less than 2 years at the reported rate

facts.label: Addressing and routing effort
facts.value: Immediate, short-term, mid-term and long-term phases

today: RFC 1380 is an Informational report of IESG deliberations. Its recommendations and timetable describe the situation and proposed work as of November 1992.

sections.title: The Growth Problems
sections.content:
The Internet had expanded beyond its original research setting. The RFC identifies three related concerns: Class B network numbers were running out, routing tables were growing, and the total IP address space might eventually be exhausted.

These problems have different time horizons. The report says that routing and allocation pressure require near-term action, while address exhaustion needs careful study before it becomes urgent. It summarizes IESG deliberations about how the IETF and IAB should proceed.
sections.plainLanguage: More networks were joining the Internet, so there were more addresses to assign and more routes for routers to track. The IESG considered quick steps for current pressure and a separate effort for the longer-term address problem.

sections.title: Address and Routing Pressure
sections.content:
The RFC reports that assigned network numbers and routes in the Merit NSFnet database had roughly doubled every twelve months. At the allocation rate described, the unassigned Class B numbers could be used in less than two years. Sites needing more than one Class C network would then need several such networks, adding routing entries.

Routing growth affects both equipment and people. Routers need memory and processing for routes, while network operators must configure and monitor policies. The document also identifies IP address exhaustion as a serious possible future problem, though its timing was uncertain.
sections.plainLanguage: One pressure came from assigning network numbers quickly. Another came from the growing lists of routes that routers had to store and people had to manage.

sections.title: Approaches Considered
sections.content:
The RFC lists possible ways to conserve Class B numbers: reclaim unused assignments, change assignment policy, or use address aggregation schemes such as CIDR. For routing table growth, it discusses more capable routers, route servers, topology engineering, charging for route announcements, better tools and aggregation.

Possible responses to address exhaustion include changing IP to provide a larger address space, using addresses that are unique only within a local routing domain, dividing the Internet into areas, or reclaiming unused network numbers. The RFC presents these as approaches under discussion rather than as a final choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The report considers using addresses more carefully and combining routes so routers can store fewer entries. For the larger address problem, it lists several ideas but does not select a final design.

sections.title: ROAD Group and Its Findings
sections.content:
The ROAD group brought together earlier IAB and BGP working group efforts to examine Class B exhaustion, routing table growth and IP address exhaustion. Its suggested criteria included minimizing changes to hosts, allowing incremental deployment and supporting a very large number of networks.

The group's preliminary report recommended CIDR for current addressing and routing problems. It also concluded that the Internet needed larger addresses, but no single proposal had yet been selected. The group called for more attention to future routing and Internet-layer capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: ROAD examined immediate scaling problems and compared candidate approaches. It backed CIDR for current routing pressure but did not choose one larger-address proposal.

sections.title: Phased IESG Recommendations
sections.content:
The IESG proposed immediate operational steps, short-term work on Class B exhaustion and routing tables, mid-term work on the address-space problem, and long-term planning for advanced Internet-layer functions. It said the phases should start together, not one after another.

The IESG endorsed pursuing CIDR because it could aggregate routes and conserve Class B numbers without changing host software. It also proposed a process for evaluating bigger-address schemes against criteria such as implementation changes, performance, security, compatibility and deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: The IESG wanted several efforts to proceed at once. It supported CIDR for nearer-term routing needs and asked the community to compare larger-address proposals before choosing one.
